newsitem.title: POLAND: Walesa says West naive over charter with Russia.
newsitem.headline: Walesa says West naive over charter with Russia.

text.p: Poland's former president Lech Walesa on Monday accused NATO of a huge blunder in signing a charter with Russia, saying the agreement would encourage Moscow to keep up a policy of confrontation with the West.
Walesa, in a newspaper commentary, took a diametrically opposed line to the Polish government, which has welcomed the deal and hopes shortly to be invited to join the Western alliance.
"I consider that the West has again committed a great, unforgiveable mistake," Walesa, who led the Solidarity union to its 1989 victory over communist rule, wrote in the Warsaw daily Zycie Warszawy.
Walesa said the agreement reached in Moscow last week by NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana would be against Russia's interests because it would encourage illusions that Moscow can rival the West.

"Solana has signed a document...which is effectively against Russia, because it creates the illusion that it (Russia) can now arm itself, cease economic reforms, because militarily it will equal NATO," Walesa wrote.
He said the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation should have driven home the idea that no one could now stand up to NATO and that Moscow should therefore focus on its economic development.

"Instead, a confrontational agreement has arisen, which talks of the equal greatness of NATO and Russia," said Walesa, speculating that maybe the Western pact had acted this way because it needed a powerful external foe.
"He (Solana) has agreed that Russia wants to be equal and blackmail the world. Tomorrow that is what it will do, when it becomes wealthier," Walesa wrote.
He said the West did not understand the former Soviet Union and reproached the Polish government for not protesting.

Warsaw's government, now dominated by Walesa's ex-communist foes, has welcomed the deal as a way to reduce tension as NATO readies to embrace former Soviet satellites including Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic, which hope to join by 1999.
However, it has said it wants to be represented on a new NATO-Russia council to ensure it has at least an equal influence to Russia's over the shaping of future NATO policy.

President Aleksander Kwasniewski, the ex-communist who narrowly beat Walesa in 1995 elections, said in the same newspaper that the deal could open the way to build a new security system in Europe and a similar one should be concluded with Ukraine, which he is to visit this week.
Walesa, as president from 1990 to 1995, advocated a firm line towards Moscow over the issue of NATO's expansion.

He now lives in his home city of Gdansk and, despite wielding some influence among parts of the opposition, has largely taken a back seat in domestic politics. He plans to form a new party after parliamentary elections due around September.
